question: What is the biggest danger when a disposable syringe is used more than once?

options.A: Immediate muscle wasting at the site

explanation: You've got this! Reusing a syringe can easily transfer contaminated blood carrying serious viruses like HIV or hepatitis to the next person. Single-use means single-use for a reason! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h1)

question: Why are unsterile multi-dose medication vials a major risk in hospital wards?

options.A: They cause immediate anaphylactic shock in patients
options.B: They attract resistant bacterial strains from the air
options.C: They harbor pathogens transferred by contaminated needles
options.D: They lose chemical potency within minutes of opening

explanation: Great thinking! Dipping a non-sterile needle into a shared vial introduces germs that multiply inside the medicine and infect the next patients who receive it. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h1)

question: Which common clinical habit is the leading cause of needlestick injuries among nurses?
explanation: Spot on! Trying to push a used needle back into its cap is the number one way nurses accidentally poke themselves. Always drop them straight into the box instead! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h2)

question: Why does a high patient-to-nurse ratio lead to more sharps injuries?

options.A: Shortages of medication force nurses to improvise injection techniques
options.B: Tired staff forget to wash their hands before starting shifts
options.C: Rushed procedures lead to hurried and careless handling of sharps
options.D: Hospitals stop supplying safety-engineered devices to save money

explanation: Exactly. When nurses are overworked and rushing to finish busy medication rounds, accidents happen much more easily. Take a breath and stay safe out there! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h2)

question: A patient visiting a poorly resourced clinic is most at risk of which hazard during routine injections?

options.A: Chronic kidney failure from sterile water overuse
options.B: Nosocomial viral infections from reused equipment
options.C: Severe vitamin deficiencies from rapid drug absorption
options.D: Permanent paralysis from standard intramuscular access

explanation: Well done! Clinics that struggle with basic supplies sometimes reuse gear, which unfortunately puts patients at high risk of cross-contamination and hospital-acquired infections. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h3)

question: Which patient group often receives multiple injections during standard antenatal care?

options.C: Elderly patients admitted for elective eye surgery

explanation: Spot on! Expectant mothers regularly receive tetanus toxoid shots and malaria prevention drugs during antenatal visits, making safe injection practices crucial for them. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h3)

question: Who is most at risk when hospital sharps are carelessly dumped in open community waste sites?
explanation: That's right! People who sort through open waste dumps often suffer accidental punctures from exposed, improperly discarded needles. Proper disposal protects the whole community. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h4)

question: What illegal practice creates a black market for unsafe injection equipment?

options.A: Melting down plastic syringes to manufacture cooking utensils
options.B: Refilling empty medication vials with local herbal extracts
options.C: Reselling repackaged single-use syringes collected from waste sites
options.D: Exporting used metal needles to international recycling plants

explanation: Spot on! Unscrupulous people sometimes gather discarded plastics, clean them up, and sell them as 'new' to unsuspecting buyers. Always check your medical supplies! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h4)

question: What is the correct thing to do immediately after giving an injection?

options.A: Break the needle off the plastic barrel by hand
options.B: Drop the unsheathed needle directly into a safety box
options.C: Place the syringe on the nearest sterile kidney dish
options.D: Place the plastic cap back on the needle using one hand

explanation: You got it! Never recap. Drop that unsheathed needle straight into the safety box right after use to keep yourself and others safe. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h5)

question: Why is changing only the needle while keeping the same plastic syringe barrel still dangerous?

options.A: The rubber plunger degrades and releases toxic chemicals
options.B: Pressure changes cause the medication to squirt backward
options.C: Blood and pathogens remain trapped inside the syringe barrel
options.D: New needles never fit securely onto old syringe hubs

explanation: Brilliant! Microscopic traces of blood and fluids pull back into the barrel during use, meaning the whole syringe is contaminated even if you swap the needle. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h5)

question: What is the very first thing you should do if you accidentally get a needlestick injury?

options.A: Wash the affected area with soap and running water
options.B: Soak the finger in a cup of concentrated bleach solution
options.C: Squeeze the puncture site firmly to force out contaminated blood
options.D: Apply a strong tincture of iodine to seal the wound

explanation: You're doing great! Immediately wash the spot with plenty of soap and running water to rinse away surface germs and lower infection risks. Don't panic—just act fast! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h6)

question: Why should you avoid squeezing or milking a needlestick wound during first aid?

options.A: It damages delicate local tissues and can push pathogens deeper
options.B: It triggers severe allergic reactions to released skin toxins
options.C: It neutralizes the effectiveness of subsequent antiseptic washes
options.D: It causes immediate clotting that traps the needle fragments

explanation: Spot on! Squeezing might feel like the right instinct, but it actually damages your tissue and can push germs further into your bloodstream. Stick to washing with soap and water instead! [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h6)
